answer: == checks whether two objects have the same value, while is checks whether two variables point to the exact same object in memory. For example, a = [1, 2] and b = [1, 2] are equal with == but a is b is False, because they are two different list objects. You should use is when comparing with None, like if x is None.
The == operator compares the values of two objects, and the is operator checks whether they are the same object, meaning the same identity.
The is operator compares the values of two objects to see if they are equal, while == checks whether two variables refer to the same object in memory. You should use == when comparing with None.

UNION combines the results of two SELECT queries and removes duplicate rows, but UNION ALL keeps all the rows including duplicates. Because UNION ALL does not have to check for duplicates, it is usually faster. Both require the queries to return the same number of columns with compatible data types.
UNION removes duplicate rows from the combined result, and UNION ALL keeps the duplicates.
UNION ALL removes duplicate rows from the combined result, while UNION keeps all the rows including duplicates. UNION is faster because it does not check anything.

WHERE filters individual rows before any grouping happens, while HAVING filters the groups after GROUP BY. That is why HAVING can use aggregate functions like COUNT or SUM and WHERE cannot. For example, SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM employees GROUP BY dept HAVING COUNT(*) > 5 returns only departments with more than five employees.
WHERE filters rows before they are grouped, and HAVING filters the groups after GROUP BY has run.
HAVING filters individual rows before grouping, while WHERE filters the groups after GROUP BY. WHERE can use aggregate functions like COUNT and HAVING cannot.

An index is a data structure that lets the database find rows quickly without scanning the whole table. It helps most on columns that are often used in WHERE conditions, JOINs or ORDER BY. The downside is that it needs extra storage, and it can slow down INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE because the index has to be updated too.
An index helps the database find rows faster instead of scanning the entire table. It is useful on columns that you filter or join on a lot.
An index is a copy of the whole table that is stored in a separate file as a backup. It is used to recover data after a crash and has no effect on how fast queries run.

A shallow copy creates a new outer object, but the nested objects inside it are still shared with the original, so changing a nested list affects both. A deep copy recursively copies the nested objects as well, so the two are fully independent. In Python you use copy.copy() for a shallow copy and copy.deepcopy() for a deep copy.
A shallow copy creates a new outer object, but the nested objects inside it are still shared with the original, so changing a nested list affects both copies.
A deep copy only creates a new outer object and keeps sharing the nested objects, while a shallow copy recursively copies everything inside. You make either one with the clone() function.

A generator produces values lazily, one at a time, instead of building the whole list in memory. A function with yield pauses at that line and hands back a value. Calling next() resumes it from where it stopped to produce the next value. This is useful for reading a very large file line by line.
Generators produce values lazily, one at a time, so they save memory. They are useful for reading a very large file line by line.
A generator is a function that returns all its values at once as a list. The yield keyword ends the function permanently, and next() restarts it from the beginning.

A p-value is the probability of seeing data at least as extreme as ours if the null hypothesis is true. A small p-value is evidence against the null hypothesis. The usual 0.05 cutoff is just a convention. And it is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
A p-value is the probability of getting results at least as extreme as the ones observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true. A small p-value is evidence against the null.
A p-value is the probability that the null hypothesis is true. A small p-value means the null hypothesis is probably true, so we accept it.

A Type I error is rejecting a null hypothesis that is actually true, a false positive. Its probability is alpha, the significance level. A Type II error is failing to reject a null hypothesis that is actually false, a false negative, and its probability is beta. Statistical power is 1 minus beta.
A Type I error is rejecting a true null hypothesis, which is a false positive. A Type II error is failing to reject a false null hypothesis, which is a false negative.

A Type I error is failing to reject a false null hypothesis, a false negative, and its probability is beta. A Type II error is rejecting a true null hypothesis, a false positive, and its probability is alpha. Power equals alpha.

Precision is TP divided by TP plus FP: of everything predicted positive, how much was really positive. Recall is TP divided by TP plus FN: of all the actual positives, how many the model found. Prefer precision when false positives are costly, like spam filtering where a real email must not be lost. Prefer recall when missing a positive is costly, like disease screening or fraud detection.
Precision is TP divided by TP plus FP, and recall is TP divided by TP plus FN.
Precision is TP divided by TP plus FN and recall is TP divided by TP plus FP. Prefer precision when missing a positive is costly and prefer recall when false positives are costly.

K-fold cross-validation splits the dataset into K roughly equal folds. The model is trained K times, each time validating on a different fold and training on the other K minus 1 folds. The scores from the K runs are averaged. This gives a more reliable estimate than a single split, especially when data is limited. Preprocessing such as scaling should be fitted inside each training fold to prevent data leakage.
K-fold cross-validation splits the dataset into K roughly equal folds. It gives a more reliable estimate than a single train-test split, especially when you have little data.
K-fold cross-validation trains the model once on all the data, then tests it on the same data K times. The final score is the highest of the K scores, which gives the most optimistic estimate.
